A necrology is a list or record of people who have recently died, usually within a specific time period or within a specific group — such as a religious community, an institution, or a profession.

Think of it as a formal death register. It answers the question: "Who among us has passed away?"

The word has two closely connected uses, and understanding both will give you the complete picture:

1. A list of deaths
This is the most common use. A necrology in this sense is a compiled record — sometimes published annually — of the names of people who have died. For example, a university might publish a yearly necrology of its alumni who passed away during that year. A church or monastery might maintain a necrology of its deceased members so that prayers can be offered for them on the anniversaries of their deaths.

2. A collection of obituaries
In this sense, a necrology is a gathered set of written notices or brief accounts about people who have died — almost like an anthology of obituaries bundled together. A newspaper or journal might publish a "necrology section" containing short write-ups about notable individuals who died during a given period.

Both uses share the same soul: a structured, formal record honouring or acknowledging the dead.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Since "necrology" lives in the same neighbourhood as words like obituary and death notice, it helps to understand the boundaries:

  • An obituary is a written account about one specific person who has died — their life, achievements, and personality. It's personal and narrative.
  • A death notice is a brief, simple announcement that a specific person has died, often placed by the family.
  • A necrology, by contrast, is almost always a collective document. It is less about telling the story of one person's life and more about formally listing or recording multiple deaths, often for the purposes of remembrance, prayer, historical record, or institutional memory.

In short: an obituary tells a story about one person; a necrology keeps a record of many.

Necrology tends to appear in formal, institutional, or scholarly settings rather than everyday speech. You might encounter it:

  • In religious institutions — Catholic monasteries, for instance, have a long tradition of maintaining necrologies so monks can pray for their deceased brothers on the anniversary of each death.
  • In academic or professional journals — some journals end each volume with a necrology section listing members of the field who passed away that year.
  • In historical writing — historians sometimes refer to old necrologies as valuable sources for tracking deaths in a community across centuries.
  • In formal organisational records — a guild, society, or club might maintain a necrology as part of its official archives.

Necrology carries a tone that is solemn, formal, and respectful — never casual. It belongs to the language of institutions, record-keeping, and official remembrance. You would never hear someone say "I read her necrology" the way you'd say "I read her obituary." The word signals a certain gravity and formality.

• The monastery's necrology dates back to the 12th century and lists the names of every monk who died there.
  • At the end of each year, the medical association publishes a necrology honouring physicians who passed away during that period.
  • The historian consulted the cathedral's necrology to determine exactly when the bishop died.
  • The journal's annual necrology reminded readers of the brilliant minds the field had lost.

A necrology is a formal, collective record of the dead — either a simple list of names of those who have died within a particular group or period, or a compiled set of brief accounts about them — used by institutions to honour, remember, and document those they have lost.
